questions.question_english: Article 13 of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR) outlines specific obligations for different levels of education. What does it explicitly mandate regarding secondary and higher education?
options_english: Higher and secondary education must be immediately mandated as free and compulsory for all citizens by statute.
Secondary and higher education must be completely privatized and managed by independent non-state entities.
Generally accessible to all by appropriate means, including progressive introduction of free education.
Advanced education is an exclusive privilege reserved strictly for students demonstrated to be intellectually gifted.
questions.explanation_english:
**Article 13(2) of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR), 1966** establishes a clear legal distinction between the state's obligations across educational levels:

1. **Primary Education (Article 13(2)(a)):** Shall be compulsory and available free to all. This is an **immediate obligation** (minimum core obligation).
2. **Secondary Education (Article 13(2)(b)):** In its different forms, including technical and vocational secondary education, shall be made generally available and accessible to all by every appropriate means, and in particular by the **progressive introduction of free education**.
3. **Higher Education (Article 13(2)(c)):** Shall be made equally accessible to all, on the basis of capacity, by every appropriate means, and in particular by the **progressive introduction of free education**.

While primary education must be universally free and compulsory immediately, secondary and higher levels are subject to **progressive realization** (Article 2(1) ICESCR) based on maximum available resources, with an affirmative duty to progressively eliminate tuition fees.
questions.explanation_hindi:
**आर्थिक, सामाजिक और सांस्कृतिक अधिकारों पर अंतर्राष्ट्रीय प्रसंविदा (ICESCR), 1966 का अनुच्छेद 13(2)** विभिन्न शैक्षणिक स्तरों पर राज्यों के दायित्वों में स्पष्ट अंतर करता है:

1. **प्राथमिक शिक्षा (अनुच्छेद 13(2)(a)):** यह सभी के लिए अनिवार्य और पूर्णतः निःशुल्क होगी। यह राज्य का एक **तात्कालिक दायित्व (Immediate Core Obligation)** है।
2. **माध्यमिक शिक्षा (अनुच्छेद 13(2)(b)):** तकनीकी और व्यावसायिक माध्यमिक शिक्षा सहित इसके विभिन्न रूपों को हर उपयुक्त साधन द्वारा, और विशेष रूप से **निःशुल्क शिक्षा के क्रमिक प्रारंभ (Progressive Introduction of Free Education)** द्वारा, सभी के लिए सामान्यतः उपलब्ध और सुलभ बनाया जाएगा।
3. **उच्च शिक्षा (अनुच्छेद 13(2)(c)):** क्षमता के आधार पर, हर उपयुक्त साधन द्वारा, और विशेष रूप से निःशुल्क शिक्षा के क्रमिक प्रारंभ द्वारा, सभी के लिए समान रूप से सुलभ बनाई जाएगी।

इस प्रकार, प्राथमिक शिक्षा जहां तत्काल वैधानिक रूप से निःशुल्क होनी आवश्यक है, वहीं माध्यमिक और उच्च शिक्षा 'क्रमिक प्राप्ति' (Progressive Realization) के सिद्धांत के अंतर्गत आती है, जिसमें राज्य उपलब्ध संसाधनों के अनुसार उत्तरोत्तर निःशुल्क शिक्षा लागू करने के लिए बाध्य हैं।
key_facts: Printed answer key: (C) Generally accessible to all by appropriate means, including progressive introduction of free education.

Answer explanation extracted from supplied reference material: means, including progressive introduction of free education. Article 13 of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights recognizes that while primary education must be free and compulsory, secondary and higher education should be made generally accessible to all by appropriate means. Specifically, it mandates the progressive introduction of free education at secondary and higher academic levels.

questions.question_english: In educational sociology, the 'hidden curriculum' refers to the unwritten, unofficial, and often unintended lessons, values, and perspectives that students absorb in school. Why is the hidden curriculum considered critical in Human Rights Education (HRE)?
options_english: It provides covert legal strategies that permit students to bypass administrative school disciplinary codes.
Authoritarian or inequitable unwritten institutional practices actively undermine formal human rights instruction.
It constitutes the sole pedagogically viable technique to introduce complex international treaties to primary learners.
It completely replaces the structural administrative requirement for formal written academic assessment in schools.
questions.explanation_english: The concept of the 'hidden curriculum' in educational sociology refers to the unwritten, unofficial, implicit, and often unintended lessons, values, attitudes, and cultural perspectives that students absorb within an educational institution. In the context of Human Rights Education (HRE), the hidden curriculum is critically decisive because formal teaching regarding fundamental rights, human dignity, equality, and mutual respect can be completely neutralized or negated if the school's informal practices, administrative authority structures, disciplinary procedures, and social hierarchies are authoritarian, discriminatory, or exclusionary. For instance, if teachers preach democratic participation and equality in class but arbitrarily suppress student expression, humiliate students, or show gender or caste favoritism, students internalize these hierarchical and unfair practices rather than the formal syllabus. Effective HRE necessitates institutional coherence, where school governance, code of conduct, teacher behavior, and day-to-day organizational culture embody human rights principles ('Education through human rights').
questions.explanation_hindi: शिक्षा के समाजशास्त्र में 'प्रच्छन्न पाठ्यचर्या' (Hidden Curriculum) से तात्पर्य उन अलिखित, अनौपचारिक और अंतर्निहित पाठों, मूल्यों, दृष्टिकोणों और सांस्कृतिक व्यवहारों से है, जिसे छात्र विद्यालयी परिवेश में अनजाने या स्वाभाविक रूप से सीखते हैं। मानवाधिकार शिक्षा (HRE) में प्रच्छन्न पाठ्यचर्या अत्यंत महत्वपूर्ण है, क्योंकि यदि विद्यालय की प्रशासनिक संस्कृति, अनुशासनात्मक नीतियां और शिक्षकों का वास्तविक व्यवहार सत्तावादी (authoritarian), भेदभावपूर्ण या अन्यायपूर्ण है, तो यह कक्षा में पढ़ाए जाने वाले मानवाधिकारों और समानता के औपचारिक सिद्धांतों को पूरी तरह निष्प्रभावी कर देता है। मानवाधिकार शिक्षा केवल 'मानवाधिकारों के बारे में शिक्षा' (Education about human rights) तक सीमित नहीं है, बल्कि यह 'मानवाधिकारों के माध्यम से शिक्षा' (Education through human rights) पर बल देती है, जिसके तहत विद्यालय के दैनिक आचरण, प्रशासनिक निर्णयों और संस्थागत संस्कृति में समानता, मानवीय गरिमा और निष्पक्षता का प्रत्यक्ष प्रदर्शन होना अनिवार्य है।
key_facts: Printed answer key: (B) Authoritarian or unfair unwritten practices undermine formal human rights teaching.

Answer explanation extracted from supplied reference material: The “hidden curriculum” encompasses the unwritten social norms, institutional rules, and implicit behaviors modeled within schools. If an institution practices authoritarian discipline, social exclusion, or unfair bias, this hidden curriculum directly contradicts formal classroom teaching on human rights, demonstrating why administrative culture and hidden practices must actively reflect rights principles.

Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
Assertion (A): Child rights under international frameworks are widely categorized using the "3 Ps" model: Provision, Protection, and Participation.
Reason (R): The UNCRC recognizes that children not only need protective care and basic provisions, but are also active subjects of rights entitled to be heard and participate in decisions affecting their lives in accordance with their evolving capacities.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer:
options_english: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation_english:
Assertion (A) is true:
The United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC, 1989) is universally structured around the '3 Ps' framework:
1. Provision: Rights to resources necessary for survival and development, including healthcare, adequate nutrition, clean water, housing, and education (e.g., Articles 24, 27, 28).
2. Protection: Rights ensuring safety from violence, abuse, neglect, trafficking, sexual exploitation, and hazardous work (e.g., Articles 19, 32, 34, 36).
3. Participation: Rights granting children civil agency to express views, assemble peacefully, seek information, and be heard in all judicial and administrative proceedings affecting them (Articles 12, 13, 14, 15).

Reason (R) is true and directly explains Assertion (A):
Prior international treaties viewed children as passive beneficiaries needing welfare and protection. The paradigm shift introduced by the UNCRC—specifically under Article 12 (the Right to be Heard) read with Article 5 (the Evolving Capacities of the child)—established that children are active rights-holders with the right to participate in matters concerning their welfare. This recognition directly led to the inclusion of 'Participation' alongside Provision and Protection, forming the '3 Ps' framework.

Therefore, Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A. Option (A) is correct.
questions.explanation_hindi:
अभिकथन (A) सही है:
संयुक्त राष्ट्र बाल अधिकार अभिसमय (UNCRC, 1989) के तहत बाल अधिकारों को व्यापक रूप से '3 Ps' (तीन पी) के विश्लेषणात्मक मॉडल में वर्गीकृत किया जाता है:
1. प्रावधान (Provision): बच्चों के अस्तित्व और समुचित शारीरिक-बौद्धिक विकास के अधिकार—जैसे स्वास्थ्य सेवाएं, पौष्टिक भोजन, सुरक्षित पेयजल, आवास तथा गुणवत्तापूर्ण शिक्षा (अनुच्छेद 24, 27, 28 आदि)।
2. संरक्षण (Protection): बच्चों को हिंसा, शोषण, शारीरिक-मानसिक दुर्व्यवहार, बाल श्रम और बाल तस्करी से सुरक्षित रखने के अधिकार (अनुच्छेद 19, 32, 34, 36 आदि)।
3. सहभागिता (Participation): बच्चों को अपनी राय व्यक्त करने, सूचना प्राप्त करने तथा अपने जीवन व भविष्य को प्रभावित करने वाले निर्णयों में शामिल होने का अधिकार (अनुच्छेद 12, 13, 14, 15 आदि)।

कारण (R) सही है और अभिकथन (A) की सही व्याख्या करता है:
1989 से पूर्व की संधियां बच्चों को केवल देखरेख का 'निष्क्रिय प्राप्तकर्ता' मानती थीं। UNCRC का सबसे क्रांतिकारी योगदान यह था कि इसने अनुच्छेद 12 (सुने जाने का अधिकार) और अनुच्छेद 5 (विकसित होती क्षमताएं) के माध्यम से बच्चे को 'सक्रिय अधिकार-धारक' (active subject of rights) का दर्जा दिया। बच्चों की इस सहभागिता को मान्यता देने के कारण ही 'Provision' और 'Protection' के साथ 'Participation' को तीसरे स्तंभ के रूप में जोड़कर '3 Ps' ढांचा तैयार हुआ।

अतः A और R दोनों सही हैं तथा R, A की सही व्याख्या करता है। सही उत्तर विकल्प (A) है।
key_facts: Printed answer key: (A) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A

Answer explanation extracted from supplied reference material: Child rights frameworks utilize the “3 Ps” model: Provision (access to healthcare, education, and resources), Protection (safety from abuse and exploitation), and Participation (expressing views on decisions affecting them). The UNCRC emphasizes that children are active rights-holders whose opinions must be considered relative to their evolving maturity, fully justifying the framework classification.

Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
Assertion (A): The provisions of the POSH Act, 2013 are comprehensively applicable to all women working within a school establishment, including regular faculty, ad-hoc staff, contractual workers, and daily-wage sanitation staff.
Reason (R): Fundamental human rights protections against workplace sexual harassment are universal and are not contingent upon the formal tenure or classification of an employment contract.
In light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer:
options_english: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation_english: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct, and Reason (R) is the accurate explanation of Assertion (A). Under Section 2(a) of the POSH Act, 2013, an 'aggrieved woman' is defined expansively as any woman, of any age, whether employed or not, who alleges to have been subjected to any act of sexual harassment in a workplace. Furthermore, Section 2(f) defines an 'employee' as a person employed at a workplace for any work on regular, temporary, ad hoc, or daily wage basis, either directly or through an agent (including a contractor), with or without the knowledge of the principal employer, whether for remuneration or not, or working on a voluntary basis. Therefore, in an educational institution, regular faculty, guest lecturers, contractual clerical staff, security guards, and outsourced cleaning workers all enjoy equal statutory protection. This broad coverage reflects the universal principle of human rights: the right to bodily integrity, personal dignity, and protection from harassment is an inalienable human right that cannot be curtailed by the contractual form or tenure of employment.

questions.explanation_english:
At the time of its adoption on December 10, 1948, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) was promulgated as a United Nations General Assembly Resolution (Resolution 217 A (III)).
- Under Articles 10 and 14 of the UN Charter, resolutions adopted by the General Assembly are recommendations and do not possess legally binding force, unlike multilateral treaties (conventions/covenants) or Chapter VII resolutions of the UN Security Council. Eleanor Roosevelt explicitly stated that the Declaration was not a treaty or international agreement, but a 'common standard of achievement for all peoples and all nations'.
- However, while strictly non-binding at its inception, the UDHR carried unparalleled moral and political authority. Over the ensuing decades, it served as the conceptual template for national constitutions worldwide (including Part III and Part IV of the Constitution of India) and international treaties. Furthermore, many of its foundational guarantees (such as prohibitions on torture, slavery, arbitrary detention, and racial discrimination) have attained the status of customary international law and jus cogens norms binding upon all nations.

questions.question_english:
Consider the following administrative scenarios in an educational institution:
I. Withholding the Transfer Certificate (TC) of a student due to non-payment of voluntary development fees.
II. Denying a student participation in the mid-day meal because the student is HIV positive.
III. Searching a student’s bag in private by a teacher based on a reasonable suspicion of carrying a weapon, following standard operating procedures.
IV. Refusing admission to a child with an orthopaedic disability citing lack of ramps on the ground floor.
Which of the above constitute human rights violations?
options_english: I, II and IV only
II, III and IV only
I, III and IV only
I, II, III and IV
questions.explanation_english:
**Analysis of Scenarios:**
- **Scenario I is a Human Rights Violation:** Judicial rulings by the Supreme Court and multiple High Courts (e.g., Delhi High Court) have established that a school cannot withhold a student's Transfer Certificate (TC) or academic mark sheets over financial or fee disputes. Doing so jeopardizes the child's academic continuity and violates the fundamental right to education under Article 21A.
- **Scenario II is a Human Rights Violation:** Excluding an HIV-positive child from common school meals is a direct violation of the **Human Immunodeficiency Virus and Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017**, as well as Articles 14, 15, and 21 of the Constitution and the right to food under PM POSHAN.
- **Scenario III is NOT a Human Rights Violation:** Conducting a private, policy-compliant search based on credible and reasonable suspicion of weapon possession is a lawful, proportionate exercise of the school's duty of care (in loco parentis) to safeguard the collective right to life and bodily safety of all students and staff.
- **Scenario IV is a Human Rights Violation:** Refusing admission to a child with a disability on the pretext of infrastructure barriers violates Section 16 of the **Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act, 2016** and Section 3 of the **RTE Act, 2009**. Educational institutions are legally obligated to provide reasonable accommodation and barrier-free access.

Therefore, **I, II, and IV** constitute human rights violations.

**परिदृश्यों का मानवाधिकार और विधिक विश्लेषण:**

- **परिदृश्य II मानवाधिकार उल्लंघन है:** एचआईवी पॉजिटिव बच्चे को मध्याह्न भोजन से अलग करना **मानव इम्यूनोडेफिशिएंसी वायरस और एक्वायर्ड इम्यून डेफिशिएंसी सिंड्रोम (रोकथाम और नियंत्रण) अधिनियम, 2017** तथा संविधान के अनुच्छेद 14, 15 और 21 का गंभीर उल्लंघन है।

- **परिदृश्य IV मानवाधिकार उल्लंघन है:** रैंप न होने का बहाना बनाकर अस्थि दिव्यांगता वाले बच्चे को प्रवेश देने से मना करना **दिव्यांगजन अधिकार अधिनियम (RPwD Act), 2016 की धारा 16** तथा **RTE अधिनियम, 2009 की धारा 3** का स्पष्ट उल्लंघन है। कानूनन स्कूल बाधा-मुक्त वातावरण और समुचित समायोजन प्रदान करने के लिए बाध्य हैं।

questions.question_english: Identify the incorrect pair regarding the historical milestones in the evolution of human rights declarations and charters:
options_english: Universal Declaration of Human Rights – 1945
Magna Carta – 1215
Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen – 1789
English Bill of Rights – 1689
questions.explanation_english:
Correct Answer: (a) Universal Declaration of Human Rights – 1945.

Detailed Justification and Chronological Analysis:
1. Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR): Adopted by the United Nations General Assembly in Paris as Resolution 217 A (III) on 10 December 1948 (not 1945). The year 1945 marks the adoption of the Charter of the United Nations at the San Francisco Conference and the formal establishment of the UN on 24 October 1945. Hence, pair (a) is incorrect.
2. Magna Carta (1215): Issued in June 1215 at Runnymede by King John of England under pressure from rebel barons. It established for the first time the principle that the sovereign is subject to the law, protecting subjects from arbitrary detention (foundational to Article 21 of the Indian Constitution and habeas corpus).
3. Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (1789): Adopted on 26 August 1789 by the National Constituent Assembly of France during the French Revolution, proclaiming liberty, equality, and fraternity as universal human principles.
4. English Bill of Rights (1689): Enacted by the Parliament of England following the Glorious Revolution of 1688, limiting royal prerogative, guaranteeing free parliamentary elections, and prohibiting cruel and unusual punishments.

questions.question_english: Which of the following descriptions most accurately characterizes the concept of 'positive rights' within the international human rights framework?
options_english: Rights that strictly mandate state abstention and forbearance from infringing upon individual civil liberties.
Rights that exist solely by virtue of explicit codification within a written national constitution.
Rights that obligate the State to proactively provide material resources, social services, and developmental opportunities.
Rights that automatically function across global jurisdictions without requiring any legal or statutory mechanisms.
questions.explanation_english:
In constitutional and human rights jurisprudence, 'positive rights' (often correlated with socio-economic and cultural rights) impose an affirmative duty upon the State to act, allocate public revenues, and build structural welfare systems to guarantee a life of dignity for all citizens.
- Unlike negative rights, which merely require the State to refrain from interfering with individual liberty (e.g., freedom of speech, freedom from arbitrary arrest), positive rights require the State to create conditions and supply resources necessary for the fulfillment of basic human needs.
- Classic examples of positive rights include the Right to Free and Compulsory Elementary Education (Article 21A of the Indian Constitution, enforced through the RTE Act, 2009), the Right to Public Healthcare, the Right to Social Security, and the Right to Food and Shelter.
- In the Indian constitutional framework, the Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV, Articles 36–51) represent positive obligations upon the State to secure a social order characterized by social, economic, and political justice, many of which have been judicially read into the Fundamental Right to Life under Article 21 by the Supreme Court (e.g., Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India, 1984; Mohini Jain v. State of Karnataka, 1992).

संवैधानिक और मानवाधिकार न्यायशास्त्र में 'सकारात्मक अधिकार' (Positive Rights) वे अधिकार हैं जो राज्य पर निष्क्रिय रहने के बजाय नागरिकों के कल्याण के लिए सकारात्मक कदम उठाने, वित्तीय संसाधन आवंटित करने और सामाजिक-आर्थिक अवसंरचना तैयार करने का प्रत्यक्ष दायित्व सौंपते हैं।
- जहां 'नकारात्मक अधिकार' राज्य को नागरिकों की स्वतंत्रता में दखल न देने का निर्देश देते हैं (जैसे वाक् स्वतंत्रता, यातना से मुक्ति), वहीं 'सकारात्मक अधिकार' राज्य से यह मांग करते हैं कि वह गरिमापूर्ण जीवन सुनिश्चित करने हेतु आवश्यक सुविधाएं उपलब्ध कराए।
- सकारात्मक अधिकारों के प्रमुख उदाहरणों में निःशुल्क और अनिवार्य प्रारंभिक शिक्षा का अधिकार (भारतीय संविधान का अनुच्छेद 21A तथा शिक्षा का अधिकार अधिनियम, 2009), सार्वजनिक स्वास्थ्य, पोषण, सामाजिक सुरक्षा और कार्य का अधिकार शामिल हैं।
- भारतीय संविधान के भाग IV में उल्लिखित 'राज्य के नीति निर्देशक तत्व' (DPSP, अनुच्छेद 36-51) मूलतः सकारात्मक दायित्वों का ही संकलन हैं। भारत के सर्वोच्च न्यायालय ने कई ऐतिहासिक निर्णयों (*बंधुआ मुक्ति मोर्चा*, *मोहिनी जैन*) में इन सकारात्मक अधिकारों को अनुच्छेद 21 (जीवन के अधिकार) का अभिन्न अंग माना है।
key_facts: Printed answer key: (C) Rights requiring the State to actively provide basic social services and opportunities.

Answer explanation extracted from supplied reference material: Positive rights mandate active state intervention, resource allocation, and government action to ensure individuals can enjoy essential social and economic goods. Unlike negative rights that require non-interference, positive rights obligate governments to proactively establish institutions, infrastructure, and public programs providing healthcare, social security, adequate housing, and free compulsory education for all citizens.

questions.question_english:
Consider the following statements regarding the derogability and suspension of human rights under international law:
I. Non-derogable rights are fundamental protections that can never be suspended, even during a declared public emergency threatening the life of the nation.
II. The right to life is recognized as a non-derogable right under major international human rights treaties.
III. Freedom of movement is an absolute right that cannot be curtailed under any circumstances.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
options_english: I only
I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III
questions.explanation_english:
Under international human rights treaties, notably Article 4 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR, 1966), rights are classified into derogable and non-derogable rights:
- Statement I is correct: Non-derogable rights represent peremptory and essential human guarantees from which no derogation is permitted, even during times of war, national crisis, or public emergency threatening the life of the nation (Article 4(2) of the ICCPR).
- Statement II is correct: Under Article 4(2) of the ICCPR, the Right to Life (Article 6), Freedom from Torture or Cruel Treatment (Article 7), Freedom from Slavery and Servitude (Article 8(1) and (2)), Freedom from Ex Post Facto Criminal Laws (Article 15), and Freedom of Thought, Conscience and Religion (Article 18) are strictly non-derogable. In India, following the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978, Article 359 was amended so that the enforcement of Fundamental Rights under Articles 20 and 21 (Right to life and personal liberty) cannot be suspended even during a National Emergency proclaimed under Article 352.
- Statement III is incorrect: Freedom of movement (Article 12 of the ICCPR; Article 19(1)(d) of the Constitution of India) is a qualified, derogable right. It can be legally restricted in the interests of national security, public order, public health (such as quarantine regulations during epidemics), or the protection of the interests of Scheduled Tribes.
questions.explanation_hindi:
नागरिक और राजनीतिक अधिकारों पर अंतर्राष्ट्रीय प्रसंविदा (ICCPR, 1966) के अनुच्छेद 4 के अनुसार मानवाधिकारों को विचलनीय (Derogable) और गैर-विचलनीय (Non-derogable) अधिकारों में वर्गीकृत किया गया है:
- कथन I सही है: गैर-विचलनीय (Non-derogable) अधिकार वे आधारभूत मानवीय संरक्षण हैं जिन्हें राष्ट्र के अस्तित्व को खतरे में डालने वाले आपातकाल या युद्ध के समय भी निलंबित नहीं किया जा सकता (ICCPR का अनुच्छेद 4(2))।
- कथन II सही है: ICCPR के अनुच्छेद 4(2) के अंतर्गत जीवन का अधिकार (अनुच्छेद 6), यातना से मुक्ति (अनुच्छेद 7), दासता से मुक्ति (अनुच्छेद 8) तथा पूर्वव्यापी आपराधिक विधियों से संरक्षण (अनुच्छेद 15) गैर-विचलनीय हैं। भारतीय संविधान में भी 44वें संविधान संशोधन (1978) के बाद अनुच्छेद 359 में यह स्पष्ट प्रावधान किया गया कि राष्ट्रीय आपातकाल (अनुच्छेद 352) के दौरान भी अनुच्छेद 20 और 21 (जीवन और व्यक्तिगत स्वतंत्रता का अधिकार) को किसी भी स्थिति में निलंबित नहीं किया जा सकता।
- कथन III गलत है: संचलन की स्वतंत्रता (Freedom of Movement - ICCPR का अनुच्छेद 12 तथा भारतीय संविधान का अनुच्छेद 19(1)(d)) एक विचलनीय (derogable) और सीमित अधिकार है। सार्वजनिक स्वास्थ्य (महामारी नियंत्रण), कानून-व्यवस्था, राष्ट्रीय सुरक्षा और अनुसूचित जनजातियों के संरक्षण के आधार पर इस पर युक्तिसंगत प्रतिबंध लगाए जा सकते हैं।
key_facts: Printed answer key: (B) I and II

Answer explanation extracted from supplied reference material: Non-derogable rights represent fundamental human protections that governments cannot suspend or restrict under any circumstances, even during national emergencies or wars. Under international law, the right to life is non-derogable, whereas freedom of movement is a derogable right that states may legally restrict during public health emergencies or security threats to protect order.

questions.question_english: Under Section 38 of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, what statutory protection is granted to the Government, the Commission, its Members, or officers in respect of actions taken under the Act?
options_english: Absolute civil and criminal immunity from all legal prosecutions in perpetuity
Protection from legal suits and proceedings for actions done or intended to be done in good faith
Blanket exemption from all public inquiries under the Right to Information (RTI) Act
Complete financial immunity from statutory audit objections raised by audit authorities
questions.explanation_english:
Section 38 of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 provides statutory indemnity under the heading 'Protection of action taken in good faith':
"No suit or other legal proceeding shall lie against the Central Government, State Government, Commission, the State Commission or any Member thereof or any person acting under the direction either of the Central Government, State Government, Commission or the State Commission, in respect of anything which is in good faith done or intended to be done in pursuance of this Act or of any rules or any order made thereunder or in respect of the publication, by or under the authority of the Central Government, State Government, Commission or the State Commission, of any report, paper or proceedings."

Legal Significance:
1. Purpose: This statutory indemnity ensures that Commission members and authorized officers can discharge their sensitive investigative and quasi-judicial functions fearlessly, without being subjected to vexatious or retaliatory litigation by public servants or institutions under scrutiny.
2. Standard of Good Faith: The immunity is strictly contingent upon actions being taken 'in good faith' (bona fide). It does not confer absolute or unconditional immunity; acts conducted with corrupt motive, fraud, or gross mala fide intent outside statutory jurisdiction are not shielded by Section 38.

Thus, Option (B) correctly identifies this statutory provision.
questions.explanation_hindi:
मानव अधिकार संरक्षण अधिनियम, 1993 की धारा 38 "सद्भावपूर्वक की गई कार्रवाई के संरक्षण" (Protection of action taken in good faith) का प्रावधान करती है।

धारा 38 के अनुसार:
"केंद्र सरकार, राज्य सरकार, राष्ट्रीय आयोग, राज्य आयोग या उसके किसी सदस्य अथवा केंद्र सरकार, राज्य सरकार, आयोग या राज्य आयोग के निदेश के अधीन कार्य करने वाले किसी भी व्यक्ति के विरुद्ध किसी भी ऐसी बात के संबंध में कोई वाद या अन्य विधिक कार्यवाही नहीं होगी जो इस अधिनियम या इसके अधीन बनाए गए किसी नियम या आदेश के अनुसरण में सद्भावपूर्वक (in good faith) की गई हो या की जाने के लिए आशयित रही हो।"

महत्वपूर्ण कानूनी सिद्धांत:
1. निर्भीक कार्यप्रणाली: यह उपबंध आयोग के सदस्यों और अधिकारियों को भयमुक्त और निष्पक्ष होकर मानवाधिकार उल्लंघनों की जांच करने की स्वायत्तता देता है ताकि दुर्भावनापूर्ण मुकदमों के डर से उनका कार्य बाधित न हो।
2. सद्भाव (Good Faith) की सीमा: यह संरक्षण निरपेक्ष या असीमित (absolute) नहीं है। यह केवल उन्हीं कार्यों को सुरक्षा प्रदान करता है जो प्रामाणिक रूप से सद्भावना और विधिक अधिकारिता के तहत किए गए हों। यदि कोई कृत्य कपटपूर्ण, दुर्भावनापूर्ण (mala fide) या जानबूझकर कानून के विरुद्ध किया गया हो, तो धारा 38 का संरक्षण नहीं मिलता।

अतः सही उत्तर विकल्प (B) है।
key_facts: Printed answer key: (B) Protection from legal proceedings for actions done in good faith

Answer explanation extracted from supplied reference material: Section 38 of the Protection of Human Rights Act provides statutory protection for actions taken in good faith. It establishes legal immunity protecting the Central Government, State Governments, the Commission, its members, and authorized personnel from civil suits or criminal prosecutions for anything done or intended to be done in good faith under the Act.

questions.question_hindi: एक विद्यालय के प्राचार्य को 6 माह पूर्व एक शिक्षक द्वारा दी गई गंभीर शारीरिक प्रताड़ना (Corporal punishment) की कथित घटना पर जाँच रिपोर्ट प्रस्तुत करने हेतु NHRC से औपचारिक नोटिस प्राप्त होता है। प्राचार्य यह मानकर नोटिस की अनदेखी कर देते हैं कि NHRC के पास कोई बाध्यकारी शक्ति नहीं है। मानव अधिकार संरक्षण अधिनियम, 1993 के अंतर्गत ऐसी स्थिति में आयोग कौन-सी विधिक शक्ति का प्रयोग कर सकता है?

questions.question_english: A school Principal receives a formal notice from the NHRC requesting an inquiry report regarding an alleged incident of severe corporal punishment inflicted on a student six months ago. The Principal ignores the notice, assuming the NHRC lacks coercive authority. Under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, what legal course of action can the NHRC initiate?
options_english: The NHRC can issue an arrest warrant against the Principal for contempt of proceedings
The NHRC can issue summons requiring personal attendance and examine the Principal on oath
The NHRC can issue a binding executive order to immediately dismiss the Principal from service
The NHRC has no coercive legal powers and can only issue repeated administrative reminders
questions.explanation_english: Corporal punishment in schools constitutes a direct violation of a child's fundamental right to life, dignity, and bodily integrity under Article 21 of the Constitution of India, and is prohibited under Section 17 of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009. When the NHRC inquires into such human rights violations, it is equipped under Section 13(1)(a) of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 with the powers of a civil court to summon and enforce the attendance of any person (including school administrators and public officials) and examine them on oath. If an official refuses or neglects to comply with the Commission's requisition or summons, they are liable under Sections 175, 178, 179, and 180 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC), and the Commission can forward the case to a magistrate having jurisdiction under Section 345 and Section 346 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. The NHRC cannot directly dismiss the Principal or issue an immediate arrest warrant for contempt on its own, but it has the statutory power to summon and examine the Principal on oath.
questions.explanation_hindi: विद्यालयों में बच्चों को शारीरिक या मानसिक प्रताड़ना देना संविधान के अनुच्छेद 21 के तहत गरिमापूर्ण जीवन के अधिकार का उल्लंघन है तथा शिक्षा का अधिकार (RTE) अधिनियम, 2009 की धारा 17 के तहत दंडनीय है। जब NHRC ऐसे मानव अधिकार हनन के मामलों की जाँच करता है, तो मानव अधिकार संरक्षण अधिनियम, 1993 की धारा 13(1)(क) के अंतर्गत उसे किसी भी व्यक्ति को समन (Summons) जारी करने, उसकी व्यक्तिगत उपस्थिति बाध्यकारी बनाने तथा शपथ पर उसकी परीक्षा (examine on oath) करने की दीवानी न्यायालय की पूर्ण शक्ति प्राप्त होती है। यदि कोई प्राधिकारी या संस्था प्रमुख जानबूझकर आयोग के नोटिस की अवहेलना करता है, तो आयोग समन जारी कर उसे व्यक्तिगत रूप से तलब कर सकता है। आयोग सीधे किसी कर्मचारी को बर्खास्त नहीं कर सकता और न ही स्वतः गिरफ्तारी वारंट निकाल सकता है, लेकिन समन और शपथ पर बयान लेने की विधिक शक्ति से अनुपालन सुनिश्चित कराता है।
key_facts: Printed answer key: (B) The NHRC can summon and examine the Principal on oath.

Answer explanation extracted from supplied reference material: Under Section 13 of the Protection of Human Rights Act, the Commission possesses civil court powers to compel attendance and enforce legal cooperation. If an institutional administrator ignores formal inquiries, the Commission can issue binding summons, require document production, and examine the administrator on oath, making non-compliance legally punishable under civil judicial procedures.

questions.question_hindi:
नीचे दो कथन दिए गए हैं: एक को अभिकथन (A) और दूसरे को कारण (R) के रूप में अंकित किया गया है:

2. Role of the Investigation Division: To maintain impartiality when local police forces are accused of bias, complicity, encounter killings, or inaction, the NHRC deploys its own Investigation Division to conduct spot investigations, examine victims, record statements, and gather independent forensic and documentary evidence.
3. Contrast with Other Divisions:
   - Law Division: Headed by a Registrar (Law), handles complaint intake, legal scrutiny, and bench listings.

Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R):
Assertion (A): The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) functions as a quasi-judicial body.
Reason (R): The NHRC is legally empowered to deliver binding judicial verdicts and directly impose criminal sentences on violators of human rights.
In the context of the statements above, which of the following is correct?
options_english: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.explanation_english:
Assertion (A) is true: The NHRC is characterized as a quasi-judicial body because under Section 13 of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, while inquiring into complaints of human rights violations, it possesses all the powers of a civil court trying a suit under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (such as summoning and enforcing the attendance of witnesses, examining them on oath, discovery and production of documents, and receiving evidence on affidavits). Furthermore, its proceedings are deemed judicial proceedings within the meaning of Sections 193 and 228 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
Reason (R) is false: The NHRC does not possess the power of a regular court of law to deliver binding judgments, convict individuals, or impose criminal punishments or prison sentences. Under Section 18 of the PHRA, its findings and recommendations are advisory in nature. It recommends prosecution, compensation, or immediate interim relief to the concerned government or authority, or approaches the Supreme Court or High Court for necessary directions. Thus, A is true but R is false.
questions.explanation_hindi:
अभिकथन (A) सही है: राष्ट्रीय मानव अधिकार आयोग (NHRC) एक अर्ध-न्यायिक (Quasi-judicial) निकाय है क्योंकि मानव अधिकार संरक्षण अधिनियम, 1993 की धारा 13 के तहत शिकायतों की जाँच करते समय इसे सिविल प्रक्रिया संहिता, 1908 (CPC) के अंतर्गत एक दीवानी अदालत (Civil Court) की सभी शक्तियाँ प्राप्त हैं (जैसे साक्षियों को समन जारी करना, शपथ पर परीक्षण करना, दस्तावेज मंगाना तथा हलफनामे पर साक्ष्य प्राप्त करना)। इसके अलावा, धारा 13(4) के तहत इसकी कार्यवाहियों को भारतीय दंड संहिता (IPC) की धारा 193 और 228 के तहत न्यायिक कार्यवाही माना जाता है।
कारण (R) गलत है: NHRC के पास नियमित न्यायालयों की तरह बाध्यकारी निर्णय सुनाने या दोषियों को आपराधिक सजा (कारावास/दंड) देने का कोई अधिकार नहीं है। धारा 18 के अनुसार आयोग की भूमिका मुख्य रूप से सिफारिशी/सलाहकारी (advisory/recommendatory) है; यह संबंधित सरकार या प्राधिकरण को अभियोजन शुरू करने, मुआवजा देने या अंतरिम राहत प्रदान करने की केवल सिफारिश कर सकता है। अतः A सही है, लेकिन R गलत है।
key_facts: Printed answer key: (C) A is true but R is false

However, it cannot render binding judicial sentences or criminal punishments directly, as its legal recommendations must be submitted to appropriate government authorities for enforcement, rendering the reason false.

Assertion (A): The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) is often critically characterized by jurists and activists as a "toothless tiger".
Reason (R): The recommendations and findings made by the NHRC are merely advisory in nature and not legally binding on the government.
options_english: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.explanation_english:
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the direct and correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Detailed Institutional Analysis:
1. The "Toothless Tiger" Critique: Former Chief Justice of India and NHRC Chairperson H.L. Dattu publicly acknowledged that the Commission functions like a "toothless tiger". While it commands broad investigative powers, its remedial outputs are non-binding recommendations.
2. Advisory Nature (Section 18): Under Section 18 of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, the Commission can only "recommend" to the concerned government or authority to initiate prosecution, pay interim relief, or take departmental action. The government is obliged only to examine the report and communicate an Action Taken Report (ATR) within one month. If the government rejects or fails to implement the recommendations, the NHRC possesses no contempt powers or enforcement mechanisms to compel compliance.
3. Jurisdictional Limitations: Furthermore, under Section 19, its powers regarding armed forces are limited to seeking a report from the Central Government, and under Section 36(2), it cannot inquire into matters after the expiry of one year from the date of the incident. These statutory limitations directly justify why it is labeled a toothless tiger.
questions.explanation_hindi:
अभिकथन (A) और कारण (R) दोनों पूर्णतः सत्य हैं, तथा कारण (R), अभिकथन (A) की सही व्याख्या प्रस्तुत करता है।
विस्तृत संस्थागत विश्लेषण:
1. 'दंतविहीन बाघ' (Toothless Tiger) की आलोचना: भारत के पूर्व मुख्य न्यायाधीश एवं एनएचआरसी के पूर्व अध्यक्ष न्यायमूर्ति एच.एल. दत्तू ने स्वीकार किया था कि आयोग कई मायनों में एक 'दंतविहीन बाघ' की भांति कार्य करता है। इसका कारण यह है कि व्यापक जांच शक्तियों के बावजूद इसके निर्णय कानूनी रूप से बाध्यकारी नहीं होते।
2. सलाहकारी स्वरूप (धारा 18): मानवाधिकार संरक्षण अधिनियम, 1993 की धारा 18 के अनुसार आयोग केवल सरकार से अभियोजन चलाने, मुआवजा देने या अनुशासनात्मक कार्रवाई करने की 'सिफारिश' कर सकता है। सरकार केवल एक माह के भीतर कार्रवाई रिपोर्ट (ATR) देने के लिए बाध्य है। यदि सरकार सिफारिश नहीं मानती, तो आयोग के पास अवमानना या जबरन अनुपालन कराने की कोई शक्ति नहीं है।
3. अन्य सीमाएं: धारा 19 के तहत सशस्त्र बलों के संबंध में सीमित भूमिका और धारा 36(2) के तहत एक वर्ष के बाद मामलों की जांच पर प्रतिबंध जैसी वैधानिक सीमाएं ही कारण हैं कि इसे दंतविहीन बाघ कहा जाता है।
key_facts: Printed answer key: (A) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A

questions.question_english: The Abidjan Principles, adopted in 2019, provide authoritative human rights guidelines regarding which specific aspect of the right to education?
options_english: State obligations to provide public education and regulate private sector involvement
International standards for the seamless integration of digital technology in primary classrooms globally
Universal guidelines for implementing standardized testing protocols across national school systems
Legal frameworks mandating the complete elimination of higher education tuition fees for all students
questions.explanation_english:
The **Abidjan Principles** (*Guiding Principles on the human rights obligations of States to provide public education and to regulate private involvement in education*) were adopted in Abidjan, Côte d'Ivoire, in February 2019 by global legal and human rights experts.

Key pillars of the Abidjan Principles include:
1. **Primary Obligation to Provide Public Education:** States must provide free, quality, public education to all persons within their jurisdiction, giving priority to marginalized groups.
2. **Regulation of Private Sector:** While international human rights law permits individuals to establish private schools, States have a strict affirmative duty to regulate, monitor, and enforce minimum standards on private educational actors to prevent commercialization, profiteering, socioeconomic segregation, and exacerbation of inequality.
3. **Public Financing:** Public funds must primarily support public education systems rather than directly subsidizing commercial private schools at the expense of equitable public infrastructure.

The Abidjan Principles have been formally recognized by the UN Human Rights Council, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights, and UNESCO as an authoritative interpretation of international human rights treaties regarding private schooling and public education obligations.
questions.explanation_hindi:
**आबिदजान सिद्धांत (Abidjan Principles)** फरवरी 2019 में कोटे डी आइवर (आइवरी कोस्ट) के आबिदजान में अंतरराष्ट्रीय विधि विशेषज्ञों और मानवाधिकार विचारकों द्वारा तैयार और अंगीकृत किए गए थे। इनका पूरा शीर्षक है: *'सार्वजनिक शिक्षा प्रदान करने और शिक्षा में निजी भागीदारी को विनियमित करने के राज्यों के मानवाधिकार दायित्वों पर मार्गदर्शक सिद्धांत'।*

आबिदजान सिद्धांतों के मुख्य बिंदु:
1. **सार्वजनिक शिक्षा का प्राथमिक दायित्व:** राज्यों का पहला और सर्वोच्च दायित्व अपने अधिकार क्षेत्र में सभी बच्चों को निःशुल्क, उच्च गुणवत्ता वाली सार्वजनिक (सरकारी) शिक्षा उपलब्ध कराना है।
2. **निजी क्षेत्र का विनियमन:** हालांकि अंतरराष्ट्रीय कानून व्यक्तियों को निजी स्कूल खोलने की स्वतंत्रता देता है, परंतु राज्य पर यह अनिवार्य जिम्मेदारी है कि वह निजी स्कूलों में अत्यधिक व्यवसायीकरण, अनुचित मुनाफ़ाखोरी और सामाजिक अलगाव को रोकने के लिए सख्त विनियामक मानक लागू करे।
3. **असमानता पर रोक:** निजीकरण के कारण शिक्षा का कोई ऐसा दो-स्तरीय ढांचा नहीं बनना चाहिए जिससे आर्थिक रूप से कमजोर वर्ग गुणवत्तापूर्ण शिक्षा से वंचित हो जाए।

संयुक्त राष्ट्र मानवाधिकार परिषद (UNHRC) और यूनेस्को (UNESCO) ने शिक्षा के अधिकार पर इन सिद्धांतों को अत्यंत प्रामाणिक अंतरराष्ट्रीय दिशानिर्देश के रूप में मान्यता दी है।
key_facts: Printed answer key: (A) State obligations to provide public education and regulate private sector involvement

Answer explanation extracted from supplied reference material: and regulate private sector involvement Adopted in 2019 by global legal scholars, the Abidjan Principles synthesize international human rights law regarding state obligations in education. They provide definitive guidelines detailing the primary obligation of states to provide public education while setting legal standards to regulate private sector involvement, commercialization, and privatization in school systems to prevent inequality.

questions.question_english: A government school situated in the capital of a State faces allegations of systemic discrimination against students belonging to a particular community regarding the distribution of free textbooks. The matter is strictly an educational administration issue under the state government. What is the most appropriate initial statutory body to investigate this specific systemic administrative human rights violation?
options_english: The National Commission for Backward Classes (NCBC)
The State Human Rights Commission (SHRC)
The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI)
The Supreme Court of India
questions.explanation_english:
When human rights violations involve state administrative departments or government schools operating under state jurisdiction, the State Human Rights Commission (SHRC) is the most appropriate and direct initial statutory forum.
Legal and Constitutional Basis:
1. Jurisdiction over State Subjects (Section 21(5)): Under Section 21(5) of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, the SHRC is legally empowered to inquire into human rights violations relating to matters listed in List II (State List) and List III (Concurrent List) of the Seventh Schedule. Education is listed under Entry 25 of List III.
2. Violation of Fundamental Rights: Discrimination in the provision of educational materials violates Article 14 (Equality before Law), Article 15 (Prohibition of discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex), and Article 21A (Right to Education), constituting an actionable human rights violation under Section 2(1)(d) of the Act.
3. Institutional Hierarchy: While constitutional courts (High Courts or Supreme Court) have overarching writ jurisdiction, statutory oversight commissions like the SHRC are designed to be the primary, accessible forum for localized fact-finding and administrative grievance redressal.
questions.explanation_hindi:
जब मानवाधिकारों के उल्लंघन का मामला राज्य के अधिकार क्षेत्र में आने वाले प्रशासनिक विभागों अथवा सरकारी विद्यालयों से संबंधित हो, तो राज्य मानव अधिकार आयोग (SHRC) सबसे प्रत्यक्ष, सुलभ और उपयुक्त प्राथमिक सांविधिक निकाय है।
विधिक एवं संवैधानिक आधार:
1. राज्य व समवर्ती सूची पर क्षेत्राधिकार (धारा 21(5)): मानवाधिकार संरक्षण अधिनियम, 1993 की धारा 21(5) के अंतर्गत राज्य आयोग को सातवीं अनुसूची की सूची II (राज्य सूची) तथा सूची III (समवर्ती सूची) के विषयों में मानवाधिकार उल्लंघन की जांच का वैधानिक अधिकार प्राप्त है। शिक्षा समवर्ती सूची की प्रविष्टि 25 के अंतर्गत आती है।
2. मौलिक अधिकारों का उल्लंघन: पाठ्यपुस्तकों के वितरण में भेदभाव अनुच्छेद 14 (समानता का अधिकार), अनुच्छेद 15 (भेदभाव का प्रतिषेध) और अनुच्छेद 21A (शिक्षा का अधिकार) का उल्लंघन है, जो धारा 2(1)(d) के अनुसार मानवाधिकार उल्लंघन की श्रेणी में आता है।
3. संस्थागत सुलभता: यद्यपि उच्च न्यायालय या उच्चतम न्यायालय में रिट याचिका दायर की जा सकती है, किंतु आरंभिक जांच, साक्ष्य संग्रह और प्रशासनिक सुधार की अनुशंसा हेतु राज्य मानवाधिकार आयोग ही प्राथमिक और सर्वाधिक उपयुक्त सांविधिक मंच है।
key_facts: Printed answer key: (B) The State Human Rights Commission

Answer explanation extracted from supplied reference material: When human rights violations involve state administrative departments or government schools operating under state jurisdiction, the State Human Rights Commission serves as the primary statutory forum. It possesses regional jurisdiction over subjects in the State and Concurrent lists, making it the most direct and appropriate body to investigate localized institutional discrimination.

questions.question_hindi: एक विद्यालय अपनी गणवेश (Uniform) और ड्रेस कोड नीति में संशोधन की योजना बनाता है। अंतिम दिशा-निर्देश जारी करने से पूर्व, प्रधानाचार्य निर्वाचित छात्र परिषद (Student Council) के साथ बैठक आयोजित कर उनके विचार, आपत्तियां और सुझाव सुनते हैं। प्रधानाचार्य द्वारा UNCRC के किस आधारभूत सिद्धांत का प्रत्यक्ष क्रियान्वयन किया जा रहा है?

questions.question_english: A school plans to formulate a revised policy regarding the institutional uniform and dress code. Before finalizing the guidelines, the Principal convenes a meeting with the elected Student Council to hear their opinions and concerns. Which foundational principle of the UNCRC is the Principal operationalizing through this action?
options_english: Article 2: Non-discrimination
Article 3: Best interests of the child as a primary consideration
Article 6: Inherent right to life, survival, and development
Article 12: Respect for the views of the child (Right to be heard)
questions.explanation_english:
The correct answer is (D). Consulting the Student Council on school policies directly operationalizes Article 12 of the UNCRC, which guarantees the child's right to be heard and have their views respected.

Legal Significance of Article 12:
1. Statutory Mandate: Article 12(1) stipulates that States Parties shall assure to the child who is capable of forming his or her own views the right to express those views freely in all matters affecting the child, the views of the child being given due weight in accordance with the age and maturity of the child.
2. General Comment No. 12 (2009): The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child emphasized that Article 12 applies not only to judicial and administrative proceedings affecting individual children, but also to institutional decision-making in schools, encouraging participatory mechanisms such as school councils, consultative forums, and student representation.
3. Democratic Pedagogy: Giving students an institutional platform to participate in policy decisions cultivates active citizenship, self-esteem, and mutual respect, fulfilling the foundational UNCRC philosophy that children are active subjects of rights rather than passive objects of management.
questions.explanation_hindi:
सही उत्तर (D) है। विद्यालयी नीतियों पर छात्र परिषद से परामर्श करना UNCRC के अनुच्छेद 12 में प्रदत्त 'बालक के विचारों का सम्मान / सुने जाने के अधिकार' का प्रत्यक्ष क्रियान्वयन है।

अनुच्छेद 12 का विधिक महत्व:
1. विधिक अधिदेश: अनुच्छेद 12(1) यह अनिवार्य करता है कि राज्य पक्षकार अपनी राय बनाने में सक्षम प्रत्येक बालक को उन सभी मामलों में स्वतंत्रतापूर्वक अपने विचार व्यक्त करने का अधिकार सुनिश्चित करेंगे जो उसे प्रभावित करते हैं, तथा बालक के विचारों को उसकी आयु और परिपक्वता के अनुसार यथोचित महत्व दिया जाएगा।
2. सामान्य टिप्पणी संख्या 12 (2009): संयुक्त राष्ट्र बाल अधिकार समिति ने स्पष्ट किया है कि अनुच्छेद 12 केवल कानूनी मुकदमों तक सीमित नहीं है, बल्कि यह विद्यालयी प्रशासन, नीति निर्माण और दैनिक निर्णयों में भी बच्चों की सक्रिय भागीदारी (Student Councils/बाल संसद) की मांग करता है।
3. लोकतांत्रिक वातावरण: विद्यार्थियों के विचारों को सुनकर नीतियां बनाना न केवल विद्यालय के वातावरण को सहभागी बनाता है, बल्कि यह बाल अधिकारों के उस केंद्रीय सिद्धांत को पुष्ट करता है कि बच्चे केवल नियमों के मूक पालक नहीं, बल्कि अधिकारों के सक्रिय भागीदार हैं।
